body.heading: Carroll's two-meaning suitcase
paragraphs: In Through the Looking-Glass, Humpty Dumpty explains the word 'slithy' to Alice: it means lithe and slimy, packed together — 'two meanings packed up into one word', like a portmanteau, the hinged suitcase that opens into two compartments. Lewis Carroll borrowed the suitcase word for the word trick itself.
The trick is simple to describe and hard to stop noticing: take the start of one word and the end of another, and stitch. If the stitch is good, the blend sounds like it was always a word.

body.heading: Blends you already use
paragraphs: Brunch is breakfast wearing lunch's second half. Smog is smoke plus fog — a word coined for London's murky air. A motel is a motor hotel. A spork is a spoon with fork ambitions. Newer arrivals include 'hangry' (hungry plus angry), which anyone who has missed lunch will understand instantly.

Some blends become so familiar that the seams vanish entirely; few people hear 'motor' inside 'motel' anymore. That is the life cycle of a successful portmanteau: it stops being a joke and starts being vocabulary.

body.heading: Invent your own
paragraphs: Try minting one. Pick two words for a thing that has no name yet — the snack you eat while cooking dinner, the walk you take to avoid a chore — and stitch the front of one to the back of the other. Say it aloud: if a listener can guess both parents, your blend works.
Keep the best ones in a notebook. Language grows exactly this way, one playful stitch at a time, and some of today's jokes are tomorrow's dictionary entries.

takeaway: A portmanteau packs two words into one suitcase — and once you notice the seams, you'll hear blends everywhere.
